card.hook: This mountain was once called London Mountain, because fog loves to gather at its base. Then the marmots won the naming vote, and it's been Whistler since the 1960s.
card.stand_here: Head to Rainbow Park on the northwest shoreline of Alta Lake and stand on the wooden dock. Face across the lake to the mountain, and you'll get Whistler and Blackcomb both in frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole slope with some lake in front. Then try 1x for a more natural look. Go to 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) for ridges, lift lines and rock detail.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the skyline on the upper third line, and leave the bottom two thirds for the lake and trees that show how big the mountain is.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day and go early or in the late afternoon, when softer light and long shadows show off the layered rock. Midday sun makes the mountain look flat.
card.selfie_here: Switch to the front camera and use 0.5x so the mountain fits behind you. Hold the phone a little low and keep the slope over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Town viewpoints are normally open public space, but the lifts and upper mountain are run by the resort, so check the official site before you go. Weather changes quickly here, so check the sky before you set out.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot with something in front, like a path or a tree line. Then zoom in and find a lift line on the slope.
card.good_to_know: Whistler Mountain sits on the northwestern edge of Garibaldi Provincial Park and was used for the 2010 Winter Olympics. Its Lillooet name is Nsqwítsu. The Whistler Peak chair serves the summit, which makes it one of the most visited summits in British Columbia.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Rainbow Park on the northwest shoreline of Alta Lake and stand on the wooden dock. Face across the lake to the mountain, and you'll get Whistler and Blackcomb both in frame.

card.hook: Picture a row of tiny cabins sliding across open air, with a whole valley dropping away beneath them. That's the Peak 2 Peak Gondola, and it looks even better from a distance, with both mountainsides behind it.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 2.2 km north-east of the gondola, and face south-west. Don't head for the Whistler Mountain terminal for this one, because that's a separate spot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the gondola line, the valley and the mountainside in one shot. Try zoom 0.5x if you want more slope and sky, or zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a single cabin on the span.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and run the line of cabins along one of them, then tap a cabin and drag the slider a little darker if bright sky or snow is washing things out.
card.best_time: Pick a clear daylight window, because low cloud can hide the valley and the far side. Check the weather and conditions on the day before you set out.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and switch to zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, so more of the view fits in. Hold the phone a bit higher and keep the gondola line and mountainside behind your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Skiers and snowboarders use the same entrance as gondola riders, so keep an eye out on the way in. The gondola is a ticketed lift and summer access depends on the ticket and season, so check the official Whistler Blackcomb site before you go.
card.challenge: Take a few frames as cabins come and go, and see if you can catch one sitting on a gridline with nothing else crossing it.
card.good_to_know: The Peak 2 Peak Gondola was the first lift to join Whistler Mountain and Blackcomb Mountain. It was built in 2007 and 2008 and carries 28 cabins. When it opened it held the world record for the longest free span between towers, at 3.03 kilometres. That record was passed in 2017, but it's still the highest gondola above the ground, at 436 metres.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 2.2 km north-east of the gondola, and face south-west. Don't head for the Whistler Mountain terminal for this one, because that's a separate spot.

selfie_research.safety: Skiers and snowboarders use the same entrance as gondola riders, so keep an eye out on the way in (Whistler Insider, Mountain Sightseeing for Non-Skiers).
selfie_research.notes: I found no page that places a visitor with the Peak 2 Peak Gondola directly behind them at a named, mappable spot, so I am not giving selfie spots or a passer-by spot. Drift Travel's 'Selfie Spot 4: Peak 2 Peak Gondola' names the gondola but gives no position, and it is about 7.5 years old. The Whistler Insider's 'right outside the Whistler Gondola doors' photo spot (Olympic rings and flags) is at the Whistler Village Gondola, not the Peak 2 Peak, so I left it out. Other photo spots that pages name (Olympic rings at the Whistler summit, Inukshuk, Raven's Eye, Cloudraker Skybridge) do not have the gondola in the shot. The only pages naming a gondola shot are the cabin side windows and the glass-bottom cabins, which are not mappable places. No page I found gives rules on selfie sticks or tripods. Peak 2 Peak Gondola operating seasons and the glass-bottom cabin waits vary, so check before you go.

card.hook: Picture the Olympic Rings sitting in front of the village roofs, with snowy mountains rising behind them like a painted backdrop. That's the Whistler postcard, and you can get it in about a minute.
card.stand_here: Stand in Whistler Olympic Plaza, about 676 m north of the village gondola, and face the Olympic Rings. Then take a few steps back so the rings, the trees and the mountains all fit in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the rings, the village and the mountains together. If the plaza is crowded and you can't back up, tap zoom 0.5x. To pull the mountains in closer, try zoom 2x (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the rings on one of the lower lines and let the mountains fill the top part of the picture.
card.best_time: Evening is the one, when the village lights and the mountain silhouettes work together. If the lights look dim, try night mode and hold your phone steady against your body or a rail.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the Olympic Rings at the north end of the Village Stroll, use the front camera (or zoom 0.5x for more room) and keep the rings behind you. For a mountain selfie instead, try Village Gate Bridge, over Village Gate Boulevard, with Whistler Mountain rising behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand beside the rings, using the rock podium there as a rest for the phone if it's still in place, while you stand in front of the rings so you both fit in one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The plaza can be busy during events and may have stage setups, so look around before you pick your spot.
card.challenge: Fit the rings, the trees and the mountain into one frame without a single stranger sneaking in at the edges.
card.good_to_know: The plaza is an open public square, and the greenery and water features make a nice foreground. If you have time for a second picture, wander into the village lanes for timber-framed storefronts and cobbled paths with mountains above the rooftops. The Covered Bridge is a quieter spot, with the icy blue creek below and mountains beyond.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Whistler Olympic Plaza, about 676 m north of the village gondola, and face the Olympic Rings. Then take a few steps back so the rings, the trees and the mountains all fit in one frame.

card.hook: Here's a museum that spent its whole design trying not to be noticed. The dark walls slip into the shadows of the spruce and cedar, so the forest ends up as the star and the building plays the quiet backdrop.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Audain Art Museum, where the phone icon marks the centre of the building. Walk out to the edge of the building or the grounds, step well back, and face the long side of the building so the whole length is in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze in the long building and the trees around it. Switch to 1x for a natural look at the walls and entrance, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the cladding and wood details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the roof and wall edges with them so the building looks nice and level.
card.best_time: Go on a cloudy day or in the morning. The soft, even light suits the dark walls and avoids harsh patches under the trees.
card.selfie_here: Leave the entry porch and head straight down the outdoor stair that runs under the building toward the meadow of tall grasses. Pose on the stair or at the meadow edge with the building behind you, using the front camera at 0.5x so the museum and forest both fit over your shoulder. Check the framing on the spot. Another option is the wooden steps at the back of the building, near the trees and the sheltered seating area.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Village Stroll northeast of Village Park, where the entrance portico and bridge are visible, while you stand on or near the bridge so they can get the whole building in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash isn't allowed inside, and non-flash photos and video are for personal use only. Selfie sticks aren't allowed in as personal items. Special exhibitions may have extra photo limits, and professional or commercial shoots must be booked in advance, so check signs and the official site.
card.challenge: Take three photos: one wide shot, one close-up of wood texture, and one with a tree trunk framing the edge. Then pick your favourite.
card.good_to_know: The Audain Art Museum is a private museum that holds Michael Audain's collection, with a big permanent display of art from coastal British Columbia. Patkau Architects designed it and it opened in 2016. Only one tree was removed in the first phase of construction, and the building won a 2018 RIBA Award for International Excellence. It's also on the Fitzsimmons Creek floodplain, so flood risk and Whistler's heavy snowfall shaped the design.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Audain Art Museum, where the phone icon marks the centre of the building. Walk out to the edge of the building or the grounds, step well back, and face the long side of the building so the whole length is in front of you.

selfie_spots.why: The stair and meadow put the dark-metal building in frame with the forest and grasses around it, which suits a selfie with the museum as backdrop.

card.hook: Picture Whistler and Blackcomb hanging upside down in a sheltered forest lake, and you holding your breath so nothing wobbles the reflection. That's Lost Lake on a calm day.
card.stand_here: Head for the floating dock in Lost Lake Park. From the parking lot, follow the path up the right-hand side of the lake, then face out across the water towards the mountains.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the lake, the reflections and the peaks in one shot. Try 0.5x to get the dock planks in the foreground, or 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the peaks across the water.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the mountains, then drag the slider down a little to make the picture darker, so the sky keeps its colour and the reflections stay clear.
card.best_time: Evening is the favourite time, with lovely light on the calm water. Summer gets busy, so arrive early or late if you want a clear view. For the sandy beach, go at golden hour.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the floating dock, where the view of Whistler Mountain is the star. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it low and a bit out, so the mountain and water sit over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The park's swimming docks were historically the nude sunbathing area, so be mindful of who ends up in your frame. Parking nearby is limited and arrangements can vary, so check on the day.
card.challenge: Wait for the perfect still moment, when the ripples stop and the mountains look like they're printed on the water, then snap it.
card.good_to_know: Lost Lake sits in woodland inside Lost Lake Park, part of Whistler's municipal park system. In winter the park doubles as cross-country skiing trails. There are several public docks, and the shoreline walk is a quieter way to get forest and lake with fewer people in the shot.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the floating dock in Lost Lake Park. From the parking lot, follow the path up the right-hand side of the lake, then face out across the water towards the mountains.

selfie_spots.why: It provides stunning reflective views of Whistler Mountain in the distance, and a Whistler selfie guide says the lake dock has a view of Whistler Mountain that really puts life into perspective.

card.hook: Five bold Olympic Rings, an open plaza and a wall of mountains behind them: this is one of those rare spots where the postcard shot is also the easy shot. Don't be surprised if someone is already posing, so bring a little patience.
card.stand_here: Stand at Whistler Olympic Plaza entrance, right by the Olympic Rings, where the phone icon sits on the map. Face the rings and take a few steps back so the plaza and mountains rise behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the rings and the mountains fit together. Switch to 0.5x for big group shots when you can't step back, and try 2x on the mountains alone for a tighter view without the rings.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the rings on a lower line and leave the mountains in the top part of the frame, then tap the rings so they stay sharp.
card.best_time: Winter is the best season, when the plaza can glow in alpenglow. Check the event schedule first, because summer concerts can crowd the plaza and winter rinks can block some angles.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the five rings at the plaza entrance (off Village Stroll, across from Day Lot 4), with the plaza behind you. Use the front camera, or 0.5x for a group, and keep the rings and the mountains in view.
card.rules_and_safety: Please don't climb on the Olympic Rings. Events can affect access to parts of the plaza, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot with the rings, then spin around and take one of the quiet open lawn with no rings at all. Which one would you pick for your postcard?
card.good_to_know: The rings stand at the plaza entrance, though guides disagree on exactly where. The City of Whistler places them at the entrance to the former medals plaza, others say beside it. Guides also suggest using the rock podium in front of the rings as a camera stand for group shots. It's free to visit.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Whistler Olympic Plaza entrance, right by the Olympic Rings, where the phone icon sits on the map. Face the rings and take a few steps back so the plaza and mountains rise behind them.

selfie_spots.name: Olympic Rings at the entrance to Whistler Olympic Plaza
selfie_spots.detail: Stand in front of the five interlocking rings at the plaza entrance, with the plaza behind you (off Village Stroll, across from Day Lot 4)
selfie_spots.why: The rings sit at the plaza entrance and are a long-standing favourite for photos, and visitors often pose there with the plaza and mountains in view.

card.hook: There's a wooden pier at Rainbow Park that does half your job for you. It points out over the water and straight up toward the peaks, so even a quick snap looks planned.
card.stand_here: Stand in Rainbow Park on Alta Lake's northwest shore and walk out onto the long pier. The directions put the lake about 670 m to the south, roughly an 8 to 9 minute walk, so face south over the water with Whistler and Blackcomb rising behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the pier, water and mountains all fit. Try zoom 0.5x to make the pier look longer, or zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pull the mountains closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the pier along a line, then tap the mountains and slide it a touch darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or around sunset, when the light is warm and the water is calmest. In autumn, morning mist can add atmosphere and the sun can cut through it.
card.selfie_here: Walk out on the wooden dock at Rainbow Park and turn so the lake is behind you. It's especially popular at sunset, when the calm water mirrors the peaks. Use the front camera and hold it a little low so the mountains sit over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep a safe distance from wildlife such as bears and deer, which are sometimes seen near the lake.
card.challenge: Take one shot with the pier running down a gridline and not a single person on it. In summer, that takes a little patience.
card.good_to_know: Alta Lake was first called Summit Lake, but it was renamed to avoid confusion with the many other Summit Lakes in British Columbia. Its new name comes from a Spanish word meaning "high up", and the lake sits at about 642 metres above sea level. It stretches roughly 2.2 km north to south, and at the north end you can still find cabins from the old Rainbow Lodge resort.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Rainbow Park on Alta Lake's northwest shore and walk out onto the long pier. The directions put the lake about 670 m to the south, roughly an 8 to 9 minute walk, so face south over the water with Whistler and Blackcomb rising behind it.
